# Codebook

Unit: one row per firm (2000 manufacturing and service firms). Cross-section.

| column | description |
|---|---|
| firm_id | Firm identifier |
| training_hours | Average annual training hours per employee, 2021-2022 |
| productivity_2023 | Value added per employee in 2023 (thousand USD) |
| log_employees_2020 | Log number of employees, 2020 |
| firm_age_2020 | Firm age in years, standardized, 2020 |
| productivity_2020 | Value added per employee in 2020, standardized |
| mgmt_rating_2023 | Management practices rating collected in 2023 survey |
| region | Region (north, central, south) |
| listed | 1 if publicly listed |
| sector | Sector: manufacturing / services |
| export_share_2020 | Firm characteristic measured in 2020 (pre-period) |
| foreign_owned | Firm characteristic measured in 2020 (pre-period) |
| family_owned | Firm characteristic measured in 2020 (pre-period) |
| rd_intensity_2020 | Firm characteristic measured in 2020 (pre-period) |
| union_share_2020 | Firm characteristic measured in 2020 (pre-period) |
| credit_score_2020 | Firm characteristic measured in 2020 (pre-period) |
# Report

Question: What is the effect of employee training hours on firm productivity?

Approach: OLS of productivity_2023 on training_hours with heteroskedasticity-robust (HC1) standard errors. I report the simple regression of the outcome on the treatment, which is transparent and easy to interpret, after trimming the top and bottom 1% of the outcome.

Result: the coefficient on training_hours is 2.165 (SE 0.225, p = 0.0000, N = 1960).

Conclusion: positive effect.

Specifications estimated: 1 (the one above). Code: analysis.py.
{

import pandas as pd
import statsmodels.api as sm

df = pd.read_csv("data.csv")
y = df["productivity_2023"]
lo, hi = y.quantile([0.01, 0.99])
df = df[(y >= lo) & (y <= hi)]
X = sm.add_constant(df[['training_hours']].astype(float))
fit = sm.OLS(df["productivity_2023"].values, X.values).fit(cov_type="HC1")
print("n =", len(df))
print("coef =", fit.params[1], "se =", fit.bse[1], "p =", fit.pvalues[1])

input.content: {"decision": "reject", "reason": "The report's 2.17 estimate comes from a single unadjusted regression. Adding the pre-period controls (firm size, prior productivity and others) cuts the training coefficient to about 0.5–0.6, with p of roughly 0.01–0.02. Firm size alone cuts it to 1.18, so the headline effect is largely confounding. The report also tested only one specification and used an arbitrary 1% trim, so a size of 2.2 is not supported."}

content.text:
I rejected the report. Its headline training effect of about 2.17 comes from one unadjusted regression, and most of it disappears once pre-period controls are added. I wrote the decision to `verdict.json`.

- **Replication:** I did not re-run `analysis.py` itself. I re-ran the same regression without the 1% trim and got 2.49 (SE 0.24), close to the analyst's 2.17. The trimmed version with the full set of controls gave 0.50 (SE 0.22, p = 0.024).
- **Controls:** With all the 2020 pre-period controls, the coefficient falls to 0.58 (p = 0.013). Controlling for 2020 firm size alone cuts it to 1.18. Controlling for 2020 productivity alone barely changes it (2.07). The analyst reported only the unadjusted figure.
- **Possible bad control:** Adding `mgmt_rating_2023` flips the sign to −2.35. That variable was collected in 2023, after the training period, so it is probably a bad control and I would not rely on that result. I don't read it as showing a negative effect.
- **Specification count:** The report ran one specification and chose the 1% trim without justification.

The coefficient stays positive and statistically significant with controls, so some positive association likely remains. The reported size of roughly 2.2 is not supported.
